title: About
text:
Course Overview
This course offers a rigorous methodological foundation in the processing and analysis of T1-weighted (T1w) Magnetic Resonance Imaging data. Designed specifically for graduate-level researchers, the curriculum moves beyond push-button analysis to provide a deep understanding of the biophysical principles, mathematical transformations, and computational pipelines essential for modern neuroimaging. By the end of the term, students will possess the technical autonomy to transform raw scanner data into high-quality, reproducible anatomical insights.


Curriculum & Objectives
The course is structured to follow the logical lifecycle of an MRI project, beginning with the physics of signal acquisition and ending with the implementation of standardized, large-scale pipelines. Students will engage with both the theoretical “why” and the practical “how” of structural processing through the following modules:

Data Fundamentals: Navigating the transition from clinical DICOM structures to research-standard NIfTI formats.
Preprocessing & Signal Correction: Identifying and correcting for magnetic field inhomogeneity, and mastering the nuances of “brain extraction” (skull-stripping) using multiple algorithmic approaches.
Spatial Normalization: A deep dive into the mathematics of rigid, affine, and diffeomorphic transformations, and the critical role of standardized templates (MNI and Talairach) in group-level analysis.
Automated Segmentation & Parcellation: Utilizing ANTs (Advanced Normalization Tools) and FreeSurfer to execute tissue segmentation, cortical reconstruction, and the generation of region-of-interest (ROI) maps.



Research Application
The primary goal of this course is to prepare students for the demands of contemporary, open-science research environments. We emphasize teaching students how to leverage robust, “best-practice” workflows that ensure transparency and reproducibility in their findings. Whether students are focusing on morphometric volume studies, surface-based cortical thickness analysis, or providing anatomical constraints for functional data, this course provides the necessary expertise to navigate the landscape of structural neuroimaging with precision and clinical relevance.

title: MRI Analyses: anatomic
text:
Welcome!
The leap from simply “running a script” to mastering a workflow is the hallmark of a serious neuroimaging researcher. This course demystifies T1-weighted processing, grounding your work in the biophysical principles and mathematical transformations, from NIfTI conversion to diffeomorphic registration, that turn raw data into anatomical discovery. By mastering tools like ANTs and FreeSurfer, you move beyond passive button-pushing toward true technical autonomy.
Our mission is to equip you with the transparency and reproducibility required to defend your methodological choices with confidence in any peer-review or clinical setting.

title: T1-Weighted Signal

title: T1-Weighted Signal
text:
T1 vs T2 contrast



T2: Capitalize on T2 decay
T1?

Wait for T1 recovery
Inversion Pulse (repetition time)
Short TE







The basic IR pulse sequence with M z then M xy plotted against time. After the initial 90° pulse from the preceding cycle of the pulse sequence the longitudinal magnetization M z is zero. It recovers with time constant T 1 and is inverted by the 180° pulse. M z then recovers during TI. When the second 90° pulse shown is applied M z becomes M xy . This decays with time constant T 2 during TE and is detected during the data collection (dc). Plots for fat (F), white matter (W) and gray matter (G) are shown. The signal shown on the image is proportional to the magnitude of M xy for F, W and G at the time of the dc. Each cycle of the sequence is described as beginning with a 180° pulse which is then followed after TI by a 90° pulse.
